blocks.text: 1. ColBERT

blocks.alt: Query tokens go through late interaction with document tokens

blocks.text: ColBERT offers a distinct third option: a middle ground technique between bi-encoders and cross encoders.
It keeps one embedding per token instead of collapsing a chunk into a single vector, a token level approach.
2. Neither Extreme
Bi-encoders compress everything into one vector each; cross encoders process everything jointly.
ColBERT sits deliberately between those two extremes.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Model type","Position on the spectrum"],"rows":[["Bi-encoder","Fastest, one vector per chunk"],["ColBERT","Middle ground, one vector per token"],["Cross encoder","Most precise, joint processing"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Token Level Embeddings Instead Of One Vector

blocks.alt: A document gets one embedding per token

blocks.text: As with the single vector representation per chunk in Dense Retrieval, a single chunk vector compresses away token level detail.
ColBERT keeps a separate embedding for every individual token in the chunk instead.
4. Late Interaction Explained

blocks.alt: Query tokens interact late with document tokens

blocks.text: Query and chunk tokens still get embedded independently, like a bi-encoder.
The interaction between them happens later, by comparing token embeddings directly against each other.
5. MaxSim Scoring Mechanism

blocks.alt: A query token takes the max similarity to any document token

blocks.text: Each query token finds its single best matching chunk token, and those best matches get summed.
That summed score becomes the final relevance score for the whole chunk.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: A query token like "refund" finds its single closest matching token embedding within the chunk, and this maximum similarity, repeated and summed across every query token, produces ColBERT's final score.

blocks.text: 6. Partial Precomputing Still Possible

blocks.alt: Document token embeddings are precomputed offline

blocks.text: As with why precomputing changes everything in Bi-Encoder, chunk token embeddings can still be computed once and stored ahead of time.
Only the final MaxSim comparison needs to happen at query time.
7. Storage Cost Of Token Level Vectors

blocks.alt: One vector per document is compared against one vector per token

blocks.text: As with the storage cost recap in Compression, storing one vector per token uses far more space than one vector per chunk.
That storage tradeoff is the real cost behind ColBERT's improved accuracy.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: A chunk containing fifty tokens requires fifty separate stored vectors under ColBERT, compared to just one vector under a standard bi-encoder, a real multiplier on total storage requirements.

blocks.text: 8. A Compromise Between Speed And Precision
As with the accuracy versus scalability tradeoff in Cross Encoder, ColBERT sits between a bi-encoder's speed and a cross encoder's precision.
It offers a practical middle ground for systems that need more than plain bi-encoder accuracy.

blocks.text: 9. Recognizing When ColBERT Is The Right Middle Ground

blocks.alt: Needing to balance speed and precision points toward ColBERT

blocks.text: Systems needing better accuracy than a bi-encoder without cross encoder cost suit ColBERT.
Extremely storage constrained systems may prefer a plain bi-encoder's smaller footprint.
10. Worked Example
The example below demonstrates computing a MaxSim style score between query tokens and chunk tokens.

code.content:
def fake_token_embed(token):
    # Token level embedding: one vector per token
    return (len(token), sum(ord(c) for c in token) % 100)

def cosine_like_similarity(v1, v2):
    dot = sum(a * b for a, b in zip(v1, v2))
    mag1 = sum(a * a for a in v1) ** 0.5
    mag2 = sum(a * a for a in v2) ** 0.5
    return dot / (mag1 * mag2) if mag1 and mag2 else 0

def maxsim_score(query_tokens, chunk_tokens):
    # MaxSim: sum each query token's best match against chunk tokens
    query_embeddings = [fake_token_embed(t) for t in query_tokens]
    chunk_embeddings = [fake_token_embed(t) for t in chunk_tokens]

    total = 0
    for q_emb in query_embeddings:
        best_match = max(cosine_like_similarity(q_emb, c_emb) for c_emb in chunk_embeddings)
        total += best_match
    return total

query_tokens = "refund policy".split()
chunk_tokens = "our refund policy allows returns within thirty days".split()

score = maxsim_score(query_tokens, chunk_tokens)
print(f"Query tokens: {query_tokens}")
print(f"Chunk tokens: {chunk_tokens}")
print(f"MaxSim score: {score:.3f}")

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: Running this example shows each query token finding its own best matching chunk token, with those individual best scores summed into one final relevance score.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Assuming ColBERT costs the same storage as a standard bi-encoder with one vector per chunk.
Confusing late interaction with a cross encoder's fully joint processing.
Choosing ColBERT for an extremely storage constrained system without weighing the tradeoff.
Assuming ColBERT matches a cross encoder's accuracy exactly rather than sitting between the two extremes.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: ColBERT keeps one embedding per token instead of collapsing a chunk into a single vector.
It sits deliberately between a bi-encoder's single vector and a cross encoder's joint processing.
Token level embeddings preserve detail that a single chunk vector would compress away.
Query and chunk tokens are embedded independently, with interaction happening later, called late interaction.
MaxSim scoring sums each query token's single best match against chunk tokens.
Chunk token embeddings can still be precomputed, with only the final comparison happening at query time.
Storing one vector per token uses far more storage than one vector per chunk.
ColBERT offers a practical middle ground between bi-encoder speed and cross encoder precision.
